Messages.Author: Robert Goudie
Messages.Body:
I have seen a number of posts recently where reference is made (whether
knowingly or not) to a suppossed dichotomy between tournament style of
play and playing for fun. It comes up in debates about card rarity
being an excuse for cards being overpowered. It is mentioned often in
debates about whether certain styles of play are "cheap" when compared
to _playing_for_fun_.

There didn't use to be such a dichotomy, though one is beginning to take
shape now. If the game is balanced (as it should be) this dichotomy
will not exist. We should all be able to _play_to_win_ and have it be
_fun_. We should be able to play any damn deck we choose. Whether we
are at a tournament or a friendly game in a game store should be
irrelevant. There should be no need to ban anything in our playgroups
that isn't banned in tournament play. This all seems very obvious to
me. It all seems rather important to the health of the game! Go ahead,
someone tell me I'm wrong; I dare you. :)

Robert

Actually, I do disagree with you slightly. I think there will always be
somewhat of a dichotomy between tournament play and play for fun,
regardless of how balanced the cards are. This is because in tournament
play, people will be trying out decks that are proven, whereas those
playing for fun will be experimenting with new ideas. It is the
experimentation, variety and "anything goes" atmosphere that generates a
sense of fun.

One effect that tournament play often has is too eliminate slow decks. In
the last tournament I played in my (lotsa-fun) "Wynn Rush" deck never made
it to the final round because the time expired before I could oust anyone.
No-one was ousted and all players got half a victory point. This is
partly because all the combat slowed the game down, but also because the
deck (which depends on getting Wynn out), must disable my predator in
order to survive before turning to my prey. By the time the tournament
round ended, I had torporized all the vampires of both my predator and my
prey, and both were helpless. It was a great deck, but even outside of
tournaments I rarely oust anyone. They usually just resign after all
their vampires are torporized.

Obviously I would have done better with the fast "Tap & Bleed" deck that
had won me the previous tournament. ...except that one is SOOO boring.

I do agree though that unbalanced cards will be used more often in
tournament play, which will create less variety and a greater
dichotomy. So far, however, the tournaments I have played in have been
rather informal, relaxed and fun. The Magic tournaments at the same
gaming club are, by comparison, extremely tense, hostile affairs.

John Whelan

In my playgroup, there is no such dichotomy. On the other hand,
many strategies that people often refer to on this group (blood gain, for
example) are virtually non-existent. I guess the argument here boils down
to what you consider "fun."
In a recent post, Steffan (sp?) recomended I try playing less
agressive and more "fun" decks. It seemed pretty off topic, so I didn't
respond to it there, but it's pretty appropriate for this thread. So....

*****Ramble mode know engaged*****

The references to fast, aggressive decks and play style as not
being "fun" are quite erroneous. Playing with slower theme decks is like
boxing with one hand tied behind your back. You will develop strategies
and tactics that are rediculously out of place in a two handed boxing
match. While this might make for some interesting "one-handed" matches,
it isn't really the same thing as boxing. You basically need to convince
your opponent to box with only one arm, or else you are going to have a
pretty miserable time. Also, a boxer who crawls into the ring with a
"one-handed" boxer is going to have a pretty easy time, leaving everyone
able to say "two handed boxing is booring. Sure you win a lot, but why
don't you try boxing for fun instead?" The thing is, I find two handed
boxing to be a lot more fun and challenging than one-handed, often we
don't have to wait for a long judges decision, but have a quick knockout,
and get on to another match. As long as everyone you are boxing with
boxes two-handed, then the "sure you win a lot, but it's booring"
argument doesn't mean crap. You don't win a lot, unless you are a darned
good boxer. As long as box with opponents of equal skill, your bouts are
fun and challenging.

*****End ramble mode*****

Algustas

Well, if you consider that old standby, chess, brand-new things often
*are* tried in tournaments first. "Proven" is great, but also means most
of your opponents will be geared up to deal with it. If somebody has a
bright new idea, they don't want people to have the opportunity to study
it. I find that genuinely new ideas often do well in both Jyhad groups
and tournaments, although new decks often need a few games of tweaking
bofre they really go.

You never have an "anything goes" environment. Most Jyhad decks are
hopelessly unworkable in any environment (try a random sample of your card
collection and you'lll see what I mean).

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Author: ianb...@aol.com
Messages.Body:
In article <5athao$5...@redwood.cs.sc.edu>, sjoh...@math.scarolina.edu (L.
Scott Johnson) writes:

>There is no provision for resigning in Jyhad/VtES.
>Resigning is the same as being ousted, if allowed at all.

I recently played a couple of games where one of my normally sensible and
subdued friend was so annoyed with his 'shuffling luck' (maybe it was just
a crap deck but let's give him the benefit of the doubt!) and the
inability of his deck to compete because of the other types of deck in the
game that he resigned and therw in his cards. This caused some bad
feeling (although not voiced) as it basically stopped the game for the
remaining 3 players. This raises two points about Jyhad:

1. There is no scope for resigning / withdrawing if you are fed up and
want to go home! (without spoiling or unbalancing the game for the
others.)

2. Sometimes however good your deck is it will be totally outclassed by
the other decks around the table because the combination of the other
decks basically stymies yours. This happens on a totally random basis and
more often than I would like! It can be very annoying to make a new deck
which you anticipate will be loads of fun to play and which you've
carefully figured out some varied defences. Then it all goes to pot
because of what the others play. (I am tempted to think of some examples
but that might lead the thread off at a tangent!)

Anyway ...

1. Maybe some (house) rules for resigning are in existence or could be
written?

2. How does one deal with this random deck factor? Build a couple of
decks so that if you get a second game in you can change? (Not always
possible for those with limited cards.)

Ian

We've always played that if a player has to leave for any reason, (such as
the lateness of the hour) and simply packs up his cards and goes, he is
treated as though he were never in the game. No-one gets victory points
or pool for ousting him. As long as the player leaves the game for
reasons independent of how well he is doing in it, I see no problem with
this.

Chucking down your cards because you are losing, or simply fed up, is
definitely bad form. It is bad sportsmanship to thus deprive your
predator from the victory point he might eventually get from ousting you.
Giving the predator the victory point is not an ideal solution. That
victory point is one that the other methuselahs are still competing for.
Had he not received the point and the pool, he himself might have been
ousted before he could oust his prey.

There is really no excuse for it either, since there's another option.
You can oust yourself by spending/transfering all your pool away. If you
are losing anyway, this is hardly going to take that long.

enjoy the game more; I can stand a little frustration. Besides, every now
and again I win anyway and, boy, is that satisfying.
